summary.text: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, also called the West Wind Drift, is an ocean current that flows from west to east all the way around Antarctica.
Driven by strong westerly winds, it carries an estimated 137 million cubic metres of water per second, making it the largest ocean current.
Because no landmass joins Antarctica, the current can circle the continent, keeping warm water away so Antarctica can keep its huge ice sheet.

facts.label: Versus all rivers
facts.value: About 135 times their combined flow at Drake Passage

facts.label: When it began
facts.value: Commonly placed at the Eocene/Oligocene boundary

items.prompt: What keeps this huge current flowing around Antarctica?

options.label: Meltwater pouring off the ice sheet
Strong westerly winds over the Southern Ocean
The Moon's tides pulling the water
Heat rising from the seafloor

items.explain: The circumpolar current is driven by the strong westerly winds in the latitudes of the Southern Ocean.

items.prompt: A sailing ship in the far Southern Ocean wants the quickest passage. Which way should it travel?

options.label: From east to west
Straight north to the equator
From west to east
Either way is equally fast

items.explain: The current and the prevailing westerly winds greatly speed travel from west to east and make sailing east to west extremely difficult.

items.prompt: What does this current do for Antarctica's ice?

options.label: It keeps warm water away, so the ice sheet can last
It carries warm water in, slowly melting the ice
It drags the ice sheet around the continent
It has no link to the continent's ice

items.explain: By circling the continent, the current keeps warm ocean waters away from Antarctica, letting it maintain its huge ice sheet.

items.prompt: Where cold Antarctic water meets warmer water to the north, whales, seals and penguins gather. What draws them?

options.label: The warmer water lets them stay cozy
Floating ice gives them places to rest
Calm seas make hunting easier there
Nutrients well up and feed plankton and krill

items.explain: At the Antarctic Convergence, upwelling nutrients nurture phytoplankton, copepods and krill, which support food chains of fish, whales, seals and penguins.

items.prompt: At Drake Passage, how does the flow of this current compare with all the world's rivers put together?

options.label: About half as much
About the same
About twice as much
About 135 times as much

items.explain: Its transport at Drake Passage is around 135 Sv, about 135 times the transport of all the world's rivers combined.

items.prompt: Millions of years ago Antarctica was joined to other land. What had to happen before this current could form?

options.label: Antarctica had to drift to the equator
Seaways had to open around Antarctica
The ice sheet had to melt completely
New mountains had to rise on its coast

items.explain: The current formed as the Tasmanian Passage and the Drake Passage opened after the Antarctic land bridge broke apart.
